questions.question: In the metric-space definition, what must be true for $\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}$ to be uniformly continuous on $\boldsymbol{X}$?
options: For every point $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}$, a different $\delta$ must be chosen after fixing $\boldsymbol{x}$.
The two metric spaces must use the same metric function.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, one $\delta \gt 0$ works for all pairs $\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2\in\boldsymbol{X}$.
The function must be bounded on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
questions.explanation: $f\colon X\to Y$ is uniformly continuous when for every $\varepsilon>0$, one $\delta>0$ works for all pairs $x_1,x_2\in X$: $d_X(x_1,x_2)<\delta\Rightarrow d_Y(f(x_1),f(x_2))<\varepsilon$. The same $\delta$ works everywhere.
questions.source_support: The definition quantifies over all pairs in the domain using one delta.
